Cultural understanding in translation: why context changes meaning

April 18, 2023
Culture | Language learning | Languages

Cultural understanding in translation at a glance

In short

  • Cultural understanding means adapting meaning, tone and references for the reader, not only swapping words.
  • The same word, date or gesture can mean something different from one market to the next.
  • Translation, localisation and transcreation adapt content to different depths, so pick the one that fits the job.
  • A native translator who lives in the target market is the most reliable safeguard.

A translation can be grammatically perfect and still fail. The words are right, but the reader hears the wrong tone, misses the joke or takes offence at an image.

That is what happens when culture doesn't translate. Most people reach for a free online tool first, and it often misses these nuances. Here is what cultural understanding means in translation, and how to get it right.

What cultural understanding means in translation

Cultural understanding is knowing how people in a given market think, speak and behave, then reflecting that in the translated text. It covers norms, beliefs, values, customs and everyday habits.

Specialists sometimes call this cultural translation: adapting meaning, tone and references so the message feels natural to the new reader. A literal version only carries the words.

Think of an iceberg. The words are the small part above the waterline, while tone, humour, references and conventions sit below it. Our professional translation services work on both.

When culture doesn't translate: one word, different meanings

As Europeans travelled west to the New World, they took their languages with them. That is why people in the Americas speak English, French, Spanish and Portuguese, and why those languages have since diverged considerably.

French shows this clearly. France remains its centre, while Quebec has spoken it since Jacques Cartier arrived in 1534. Almost 500 years on, Canadian French differs from European French in vocabulary and accent.

That can cause real embarrassment. The word "gosse" means a child in France, yet in Quebec it is a vulgar term for male anatomy. Without that cultural knowledge, you could make people laugh or deeply embarrass them.

English has the same problem. British and American readers disagree about "pants" and "football", so a UK brand writing for the US needs more than a spell check. Our French translation services match the regional variant to your audience.

What changes from one market to the next

Culture shows up in small details that a word-for-word approach never touches. Dates, numbers, units, forms of address and humour all shift between countries.

Take the date 11/05/2026. A British reader sees 11 May, while an American reader sees 5 November. On a contract, an invoice or a delivery note, that gap gets expensive.

Formality works the same way. French has "tu" and "vous", German has "du" and "Sie", and Spanish has "tú" and "usted". Choose the wrong one and a brand sounds cold, or far too familiar.

Details translators check every time

  • Units, measurements and currency formats
  • Names, titles and honorifics
  • Humour, idioms and sayings
  • Colours, symbols and imagery
  • Public and religious holidays
  • Legal and regulatory wording

Cultural sensitivity: avoiding misunderstanding and offence

Every society has its own sensitivities. They are softening in a globalised world, but they still matter whenever you translate into another language.

Communication style and dress

Communication style counts too. In live interpreting, steady eye contact signals respect in one culture and can feel impolite in another. Dress can also cause offence, depending on religious beliefs.

For live meetings, our remote interpreting services bring that awareness into the room.

Why a small slip costs so much

A single word can change the meaning of an entire sentence, even when it is technically correct. The message may read as offensive when you never meant it to, and written words are hard to take back.

Showing cultural awareness earns respect. In business, that attention to detail builds trading relationships that last for years. Read more on why cultural sensitivity matters in translation.

Translation, localisation and transcreation: how far to adapt

Not every document needs the same depth of cultural adaptation. A contract should stay close to the source, whereas a slogan should be rebuilt for the new audience.

Use the scale below to decide. For websites, our website translation services include localisation, and our marketing translation experts handle transcreation.

How to get cultural understanding right in your translations

Work with native translators who live in the market

A translator's learning never stops. Native linguists who live and work in your target country pick up shifts in slang and etiquette long before a guidebook does. Meet our native specialist translators.

Do your research

Research is your first step in any new country. Start online, then speak with local people, who know best what you can and cannot say.

Share what you learn with your translator in a short brief. Context on audience, tone and purpose saves rounds of revisions.

Watch for local dialects

In some countries, dialects play a major role in communication. Italy is a prime example, where each region, and sometimes each city, has its own. A translator has to account for that.

Anyone handling high-quality translations needs to understand these sensitivities to convey meaning accurately. That is why it pays to specialise in a few countries rather than spread yourself thin.

Review and test in context

Ask a second native speaker to review the text where readers will actually see it, whether on a web page, a label or a slide. A quick test with local readers catches what a desk review misses.

Turn cultural insight into results in new markets

Cultural understanding is what separates a translation that is merely correct from one that wins customers. If you are planning to enter a new market, a specialist partner saves you from costly rework.

BeTranslated has matched UK businesses with native translators since 2002. Whether you need a document translation project, a multilingual website or an interpreter for a meeting, tell us about your audience and we will advise on the right level of adaptation.
